1.pericope_label: When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language: Judah was his sanctuary, and Israel his dominion

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the psalm as a finished liturgical whole, the historical member of the Hallel group and the festival psalm of the eighth Passover day, built of four tetrastichs and sung to its own tone; Ellicott works verse by verse from the Greek, defending barbarous for the strange language and arguing from a feminine verb that the second verse names the country rather than the tribe.

Gill dwells on the manner of the departure — public, willing, wealthy, and without a feeble man among them — and denies that Judah can mean a building, since no sanctuary existed at the exodus; Calvin takes the psalm as a short account of the deliverance whose design was that the redeemed should be wholly God's, and dismisses as foreign to the prophet the notion that one tribe alone was then consecrated.

Clarke doubts the poem is entire, noting the missing title, the abrupt opening and close, and its union with the following psalm in the manuscripts, and argues from the naming of Israel beside Judah that it postdates the division of the tribes; Wesley disposes of the same clause in a line, one tribe put for all.

Henry finds in the two verses a whole constitution, sacred and civil at once, and a moral in the preserved language of a people who would not learn their oppressors' speech; Spurgeon hears the opening as a burst too impatient for a preface and dwells on the unanimity of a household that left without a straggler.
Augustine declines to treat the psalm as a record of the past at all, holding that the deeds happened for examples and that what looks like narrative is prediction.

debates.question: Does Judah in the second verse name the tribe or the whole nation?

positions.view: The whole body of the people; a building cannot be meant, since no sanctuary yet existed, and the sense is that the nation was holiness to the Lord.
The whole people; the tribe takes precedency as the most numerous, but the honour belongs equally to all, and the parallel clause about dominion simply repeats the thought.
The country rather than the tribe, on the evidence of the feminine verb and of the parallelism.
The redeemed nation is so called because God made it his sanctuary.

debates.question: Is this a complete psalm, and when was it composed?

positions.view: Probably not entire — no title, an abrupt beginning and end, and in most manuscripts and versions it is joined to the psalm that follows; and since Israel is distinguished from Judah it must be later than David.
A finished and formally regular composition, four tetrastichs, with a fixed liturgical place as the psalm of the eighth Passover day.
The question is not raised; the psalm is read straight through as a commemoration of the deliverance.

debates.question: What is meant by a people of strange language?

positions.view: A stammering or unintelligible speech, which the Greek and the Targum rightly render barbarous.
The same, with the scorn ancient peoples reserved for foreign speech deliberately retained in the word.
Possibly no more than a foreign people, though the difference of tongue was real; an old English Psalter took the phrase of religion instead, reading heathen folk.
A mark of separation the people themselves maintained, keeping their own speech pure as an earnest of deliverance.

outliers.note: Refuses the historical reading altogether, and observes that the psalm reports the wonders differently from the narrative it draws on — the river driven back rather than standing still, hills skipping where the history has none — so that it might not be mistaken for a repetition of past acts rather than a prophecy.
Reports the several candidates advanced for authorship: the three companions of the furnace, Esther, and Mordecai.
Illustrates the contempt buried in the Hebrew word for foreign speech by noting that Russians still call Germans dumb.

themes: When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language;
Judah was his sanctuary, and Israel his dominion.

3.pericope_label: The sea saw it, and fled: Jordan was driven back... Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters

schools.summary: Ellicott presses the wording — fled rather than driven back, a stream turned backwards rather than parted, skipped as a word elsewhere rendered dance — and admires the suspense by which the divine name is withheld until the seventh verse.

Gill expands each question rhetorically and answers the sixth verse in a word, that the hills moved from fear and not from joy; he also reads the fleeing sea typologically of the Gentile world under the first preaching of the gospel and of the check put on sin in a converted heart.

Clarke supplies a fresh rendering of the interrogation, credits the poem's effect to the deliberate withholding of any agent, translates the flint as granite from a specimen on his desk, and appends older English and Anglo-Saxon versions of the psalm; Wesley contributes two short identifications, the mountains as Horeb and Sinai with their neighbours, and the earth's trembling as more than was fit.

debates.question: Is the verb in the seventh verse a command or a statement about the past?

positions.view: An imperative standing for the preterite; the ancient versions render the earth trembled or was moved, and the sense is that the sea and hills plead their own case.
The same; almost all the versions took it as past, and the psalmist is answering his own questions.
The imperative stands, and its literal force is to be in travail.

debates.question: Where does the power of these verses lie?

positions.view: In the poet's suppression of any agent until the wonders have all been displayed, so that the presence of God, once named, solves every difficulty at once.
In what the sea saw — that this people were God's holy and peculiar possession — and in what the miracle prefigures.

outliers.note: Turns the closing verse into a note on language and mineralogy, identifying the flint as granite from a piece of Horeb lying before him and reprinting the psalm in an old Psalter and in Anglo-Saxon to show the affinity of the tongues.
Alone reads the fled sea as a figure of the Gentile nations trembling under the first preaching of the gospel, and of the torrent of wickedness stopped in a man's heart by efficacious grace.

themes: The sea saw it, and fled: Jordan was driven back.
The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs.
What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest? thou Jordan, that thou wast driven back?
Ye mountains, that ye skipped like rams; and ye little hills, like lambs?
Tremble, thou earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob;
Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters.
